REDDING, CAL, April 29-Seymour
Bass, Deputy United States Fish Commits
sioner at Baird, pretty little spot on the
McCloud River, came near being drowned
in Pit River Tuesday evening. Mr.. Bass
had been in Redding attending the Odd
Fellows celebration, and left this city on
Tuesday for his home. He drove a span
of horses attached 10 light spring wagon.
With him we're his two sons and James
Cessna of this city, who was on his way
to Copper City to attend to some mining
business.


1t was about o'clock when the four
reached the Pit River ferry. 1t was storm
ing somewhat at the time, and the heavy
rains of the several days previous had
converted the Pit River into raging tor
rent. The water was running like mill
race when Bass and his companions
boarded the ferry-boat When the middle
of the stream had been reached one of the
cables attached to the ferry broke on ac-
count of the severe strain from the force
of the water and the large boat slowly
turned over.


One of Bass boys retained his presence
of mind, and as the boat turned he walked
over it and stood safe and rode on the bot
tom when she had rolled over. Cessna
and the other boy slipped into the water,
but soon caught hold and pulled them
selves into the capsized boat. Bass vas
less fortunate. He was carried some dis
tance awav and into an eddy The circling
water took him like leaf and with few
whirls he sank. Twice he sank beneath
the surface of the water and arose. As he
arose 20 the surface the second time the
capsized boat, which had gone nearly to
the opposite shore, dritted back, and his
companions rescued him just as he was
going down for the third and, perhaps,
last time.


After his rescue Bass remained in an
unconscious condition for about two hours
and his companions thought he would not
recover. But by hard work, however, he
was brought back to consciousness and at
length the shore was reached. The
horses and wagon were carried down the
stream for about 200 yards, when the ami
mails got loose from the vehicle. The
horses were carried on down the stream
at rapid rate and when last seen were
some three miles below the ferry. They
no doubt were drowned. 1t was a thrilling
experience, and one from which it may
take some time for Mr.. Bass to recover.

A method, differing radically from those
hitherto employed, has been devised, and
is interesting for its novelty. and is SEEM
ingly practicable. The plan is to have
the color on the sensitized paper before
printing-red, green and blue lines ruled
in alteration, 300 or more to the inch.
sheet of paper thus prepared appears
family tinted, and would almost pass for
white. The negative is made behind
colored screen, ruled in exactly the same
way. Superimposed upon the paper in
the perfect register, the negative is then
used for printing, and, owing to the chemi-
cal action which ensues, the color is fixed
wherever the light falls. and may be dis
solved off from those spots upon which
the light has not fallen. For instance,
red point in the object photographed re-
fleets ray of red light which encounters
red line on the screen before the mega
tive and fails to get through. This same
point remains transparent after develop
ment, and will thus allow red point on
the print ting paper to be acted upon and
become fixed. Similarly with yellow and
blue colors.-Yale Scientific Monthly.

Nearly the greasiest thing in the world
at the present time, says the San Fran
cisco Call, is the old bark knoch Talbot
which arrived in port from Redondo last
Monday. Compared with her Penn
SylNania oil we'll is a soda water foun-
tain and sperm whale refrigerator
car.


All the alkali in the economy of chem
istry couldn't out out" the spot that
covered the Enoch Talbot from stem to
stern, keel to truck, clew to caring Even
the winds that blow by her become lu-
bricated from their passage through the
oleaginous atmosphere and fly away all
the faster from the instant association


She is so oi.y that she floats in calm
of her own making, for no wave can hold
its own against the unctious charm she
sheds around herself.


Twenty-siX days ago the bark started
from Redondo with 5000 barrels of crude
petroleum on board. The entire interior
of the vessels hull had been fitted up
with wooden tanks, into which the thick,
tar!ke fluid had been pumped.


She had head winds. Gains and bad
weather generally, which accounts for
the long passage of twenty-four days.
A short time out from port the pitching
of the Talbot burst a tank, letting almost
1000 barrels of oil loose to roam around
the bark at pleasure.


1t may be said that that stuff, in it's
crude petroleum way, made the most of
the opportunity. When it couldn't flow
freely it seeped, and between the flowing
and seeping it managed to get pretty
much everywhere. The pitching and
rolling Of the bark dashed the oil here
and there through the hull forcing it
where even the most ambitious fluid
would not care to penetrate. 1t got into
the bilge With the water leakage. and
when the vessel was pumped out the oil
came up through the pump wei! and ran
out into the sea.


Every timber. and it seemed that
every spar, block and rope was saturat-
ed, and the Righteousness rampant in
that hold reached as high as the royal
trucks. it didn't OOze out through the
seams Of the Enoch Talbot, because she
was an old Black Ball packet, and ship
with the great black disk on her foretop-
sail was never known to wear out


For several days no particular danger
threatened the oil-logged bark. She
simply rolled along working northward,
end Captain johnson was careful not to
drop any burning matches down into
that rather inhammable hold. But the
leaning of the vessel over TO leeward
caused the heavy, thick fluid to collect
on that side, consequently the bark grad
ually acquired dangerous list.


I]VeTV hing solid that was movable
was shifted to the weather side, and the
pumps were set to work to help ease the
bark. Several hundred barrels of oil
were run overheard smoothing the sea
down for a wide distance around the
vessel. During the bad weather the
steam pump at the main hatch broke
from it's fastenings and fell into the hold,
where it lay submerged in the petro-
leum.


The bark finally succeeded in getting
off the harbor, where a tug smelled her
out, it is said. She is at the Arctic OIL
works getting rid of her dangerous and
inconvenient cargo. The old craft is all
right. but she is about the greasiest
thing in the world.

The final Growing of the roosters and the
cackling of the hens in the Tabernacle
last night was entirely swallowed up in
the volume of music that was created AT
the doors by the two rival halves of the
original Fifth Infantry band. For a
quarter OF an hour the two bands plaved
different airs only few feet apart, and
not until after conference with the di-
reetors was peace and harmony restored.


For long time there has been dissatis-
faction between the two bands. which
were originally one. Stories differ as to
how the trouble started; but about a
month ago the seeding faction, which is
styled the Oakland Professional band,
threatened legal proceedings against the
Fifth Infantry band if some music which
was joint property was not restored to the
place from which it had been taken. This
widened the breach, and when the Poultry
Show was opened both bands applied tor
the privilege of supplying the evening
music. In order to prevent any friction
Superintendent Sharpe made an arrange
ment by which the two bands should play
on alternate nights.


This arrangement was satisfactory. and
had the show closed Wednesday night, as
was anticipated, there would have been no
complication. But the show decided to
keep open another night, and by some
misunderstanding both bands were told to
report for duty last night.


The Fifth Infantry band arrived first,
and taking Up their stand at the entrance
under the leadership of Director McBain,
they commenced playing the Boulanger
march. = few minutes later the Oakland
Professional band, under the direction of
Mr., Richardson, made its appearance, and
Without paying any attention to their
rivals they took up position on the other
side OF the entrance and opened up with
one Of the liveliest of Sousa's productions
For quarter OF an hour the two bands
played, and each manipulation of a brass
instrument exhaled martial music as if his
life depended on the volume of sound
emitted.


When the exhibition officers arrived they
called the two directors into their office
and consultation was held. While the
negotiations were pending the music
struck up again and the two leaders rushed
10 The Tabernacle entrance to see who had

Canuelaria, in the province of Pinar del

lost eighty killed and many wounded. On
the Spanish side, Captain Gil is known to
have been wounded. The other losses to
the rebel forces have not been ascertained.


The lighting in Pinar province in The

since the beginning of the war. The con-
dition to which the Spanish forces in the
west are reduced has led Marin to abandon

relief OF the beleaguered towns.


Maceo's forces include the bands of Miro,

strength of 600, probably much greater

1t is impossible to learn the losses at Can

NEW YORK, N. Y, Feb. GA big
crowd of sporting men gathered in Madi-
son-souare Garden tonight despite the
inclemencv of the weather. "Bob" Fitz-
simmons, the famous middle and heavy
weight champion, was the magnet that
drew upward of 1000 spectators around the
roped arena. They not only had the op-
portunity of seeing the hero of the latest
fstic battle pitted against couple of good
heavy-welghts but he also spared three
friendly rounds with the man he bested
in Mexico few days ago. The authori-
under Inspector Brooks on hand to prevent
anything like fighting, -


Fitzsimmons, accompanied by his wife
and party, arrived in the garden about
o'clock and the champion received salvo
of applause. Brady, Corhett's manager,
repeatedly waved roll of bills which he
said contained $4,000 and tried to shout a
challenge to Fitzsimmons, but the cheer
ing drowned his voice.


Fitzsmmons raised his hat in acknowl-
edgment of his reception. A hoarse voice
from the gallery cried out: "Corbett
won't do thing to YOU" Fitzsimmons
appeared angry.


Peter Maher came in before o'clock.
Tim Hurst had charge of the stage, and
Harry Cornish of the New Manhattan
Athletic Club held the watch. Harry
Petersen and Denny Marshall started the
fun with a four-round set-to. Then two
colored champions from Moine.ta Lane,
Louis Brodie and r. Billop, pounded each
other to their hearts content, and were
followed by Matt Matthews and Dick
Behrens, who exchanged very few love
taps.


Paddy McGuggin of Newark and Johnny
Banks of New York, colored, rehearsed
their little "act." Then Joe Harmon and
Marty Delaney went four rounds, and gave
way to Billy Lee and Harry Force, who
gave lively exhibition.


Paddy Purtell, the Kansas City welter-
weight, tapped Tommy West almost at
will


Ernest Roeber. the champion wrestler,
and William Marx followed in Greco:
Roman wrestling bout, which was won by
the former.


A very fast and scientific bout between
Jack Everhart and Billy Vernon, the
"Haverstraw brickmaker," followed.





Bob in bag-punching exhibition. Mar
tin Julian was in the ring with him. There
was a storm of applause and cries of
speech" American Beauty roses were
showered upon Fitzsimmons while he was
giving his exhibition. Fitzsimmons
punched and the crowd roared. Finally
with one terrific swing the burly Cornish
man sent the sphere flying away into
the middle OF the crowd.


Fitzsimmons put on the. gloves and
started a three-roUnd bout with Paddy
Brennan. Fftzsimmons' powerful right
rained taps with lightning CELEBRITY on
Paddy's body and the unerring left was
busy on his head. But the champion was
very tolerant and his taps were love-taps
indeed.


The appetite OF the spectators was
whetted to degree when the announcer
stated that Fitzsimmons would wind up
with Maher. The Irishman has evidently
not lost his hold on the hearts of the
crowd. for he was cheered to the echo as
he stepped into the ring. Before Peter got
on the gloves Fitzsimmons stepped across
the ring and shook hands with his late foe.


Maher's eyes were still swollen and in
famed. Peter blinked when he faced
Fitzsimmons. and the latter iabbed him
on the mouth. Right and left the cham
pion shot out and caught Peter on both
sides of the head. The Irishman closed,
delivering left lightly on the body and
after some sparring the one-minute round
closed.


The second round was lively and both
did some fast work. Maher's supporters
in the audience were loud in their exhor-
tations to Maher to KNOCK him out,
Peter" was frequently heard.


The third round was quite as friendly as
the others, but the love-taps were by no
means gentle. They clinched frequently,
and once Fitzsimmons sent a straight LETT
on Maher's chin and the Irishmap's head
went back. just as the bell sounded they
were clinched and showed no signs of
breaking.


1t was stated that Brady. on behalf of
Corbett, and Quinn. on behalf of Maher,
challenged Fitzsimmons after the exhibi-
ton was over. Martin Julian refused to
affirm or deny the statements. Both Fitz-
simmons and Julian declined to make q
speech, although there were loud and fire.
auent calls therefor from the spectators.

At the meeting of the Labor Council
last night a report was submitted showing
that the following named unions are in
favor of sustaining the Labor Council as
against the Central Labor Alliance re-
Gently organized by convention of dele
gates from the various labor unions:
Sailors, Iron molders, Horseshoers'
Cigar-makers' Electrical Workers, Theat-
rical Employees, Coopers' Musicians
Brewery Workmen, Bakers and Pattern
makers.


The Tailors' and Furniture makers
unions had not vet taken action. and the
Garment-makers' and Cooks and Walters
unions were reported to be not yet regu-
larry affiliated with the council, though
they soon expect to be.


Reports from various unions were made,
showing their condition as favorable.


The following motion was adoped: That
the Labor Council is in favor of proper
tional representation, and that the legis-
lative committee be instructed to present
bill to the next Legislature amending
the constitution to provide for proper
tional representation.


On the report of the special committee
that prison-made barrels were being
shipped here from the East, motion was
adopted instructing the committee to con-
tinue its investigation and requesting the
delegates TO lay the matter before their
respective unions for additional informa-
ton. for the purpose of learning whether
any other prison-made goods were being
marketed here.

after quarrel with Sarah Crompton, the
daughter of woman at whose home he
lived, at the breakfast table. He was ex-
tremely jealous of the girl because of the
attentions bestowed upon her by young
man who lived with them. Some days ago
he threatened the , lives OF the young
couple. and brother of the girl, fearing
trouble, removed the powder from the
shells of three pistols which Reheiser kept
in his bureau.


After the quarrel this morning Reheiser
procured one OF his pistols and fired twice
at the girl. Knowing the condition of the
shells she laughed at him. Reheiser pro-
cured another pistol and shot twice again
with no effect. Then he rushed into his
bedroom and got rifle. The girl and her
mother jumped through a window and
ran for the neighboring hills.


The crazed lover fired one shot from the
Winchester, barely missing the girl as she
was going over hill. Then he went to
his bedroom, put the muzzle of a shotgun
to his forehead and fired, the charge car
rying away the top of his head.


Reheiser was 81 years old. He had been
foreman of the railway roundhouse here
for ten years and lived with Mrs. Cromp-
ton for the past seven years. His wife
lived near Hilarita. The suicide had been
drinking heavily OF late.

SANTA ROSA, CAL, May 26.-The feat
ure of the afternoon session of the Woman
Suffrage Convention to-day was a paper
by Mrs. Fannie MEG. Martin entitled,
"Does the Professional Woman Need the
Bailot?" Mrs. Martin was formerly Su-
perintendent of Schools for Soroma Coun-
ty and is now practicing law here. She
spoke from the standpoint of profess
sional woman. Her paper was largely
argumentative, but logical and keen.


Theology, medicine and law, she said,
were the three principal professions, and
their ranks were now honored by many
women who had to pass the same exami-
nations as the men to get there. These
professional women did not ask for any
easier conditions than those imposed upon
the men, but they did ask for the same
privileges. She paid nice compliment to
Mrs. Clara Shortridge Foltz, the famous
woman lawyer now practicing in New
York. Quoting the law which provides
that women should have an equal right
with the men TO practice law, the speaker
declared it to be ridiculous that they
should have no voice in making the laws
or selecting the judges before whom thew
had to practice. She closed with an APP
peal to parents to encourage their daugh-
tiers to adopt a professional career.


Judging from the great crowds that at
tended the previous meetings the lady
managers concluded that the M E. Church
would no hold all the people who desired
to hear Rev. Anna H. Shaw, and the Athe-
n@um was engaged. Fully 1900 people
were present when the Hon. John Tyler
Campbell of this city introduced the
speaker of the evening. The Introductory
speech was quite brief. and predicted the
ultimate success of the equal suffrage
movement. The speaker, who is noted for
saying graceful things about the ladies,
was evidently sincere in this instance,
when he declared that the women of the
country possessed the larger share of its
intelligence and that it was only a ques-
tion of time when they would take their
places at the bar of civil and political
equality.


Miss Shaw enlisted the sympathy of the
big audience at the outset, and at times
handled her subject without gloves. With
that peculiar grace and power that has
made her famous throughout the country,
she enlightened her hearers and exploded
the pet arguments of the opposers of the
proposed innovation.


These oyerturnings of time-frayed mas
culine objections were received with de-
light and applauded by the 1000 or more
ladies present. and will be used in family
conventions by many Santa Rosa maid
and matron during the coming campaign.

of Astoria's third annual regatta opened
somewhat inauspiciously, the sky being
overcast and there being but little wind.
Early in the afternoon. however, a brisk
breeze sprang up and all the sailing races
were completed in good time. The almost
total absence of wind in the morning
made the conditions favorable for the row.
ing races, which were well contested.


The first event was a surfboat race,
which was won by the Fort Candy life
saving crew, who defeated the Fort
Stevens men over a three-mile course in
1925

second race, which was won by one of the
Cutting Packing Company's boats.

for Whitehall boats, and the Curio of Port
land captured the event for catboats.


The sloop race. free for all, handicap,
was won by the Mayfower of Ilwaco.
which defeated her four competitors after
q most interesting contest.


The gasoline launch race brought out
seven starters and was won by the Claude
B. Manthorn.


In the race for ships boats the crew of
the British ship Sutherlandshire carried
off the honors, the Antopie's crew taking
second money.


Taylor and Wroton of Astoria defeated
Clarke and Adams of the Fort Candy crew
in double-scull Whitehall race, two Sec
onds only separating the boats at the fin
ish.


No accidents occurred during the day
and the large number of visitors were
highly satisfied with the days entertain
ment.

ness. the chief industry OF Washington, is

eign trade has suffered, but nothing in
comparison with Interstate and Eastern
shipments. What is worse relief does

rectly about 10000 men engaged. Nearly
ali the big business houses, wholesale and

BODIE, CAL, April 25.-All day long
fire has ragged in the Standard mine at the
edge of town. Columns of fame have
poured from the shafts and the heat of a
monster furnace kept at distance the
workers who endeavored to check the
contiagration. The fire started at the 35O-
foot level, and after fighting the flames
since sun-up they were got under control
at o'clock tonight


The alarm was given at 6 o'clock this
morning and long files of excited miners
and citizens began toiling up the steep
Standard Hill through the snow.


From the opening of the main shaft
volumes of white smoke were pouring with
the roaring sound of blast furnace. The
pumps at the Lent shaft were started, but
it was found that the pipes leading to the
top of Standard Hill were frozen. An
effort was made to diminish the draught by
covering the opening of the shaft with
timbers and dirt, but this was only par.
TALLY successful. Every effort was made
to check the fire underground at the end
of the Bulwer tunnel, but masses of red
hot debris came crashing down through
the shaft at intervals and the heat was ex-
cessive.


Mule teams were kept busy hauling
water through the Bulwer tunnel and sew
eral Babcock extinguishers were put to
good use keeping the fire away from tim.
bers in the station.


AS the timbers burned away in the main
shaft great quantities of rock became de-
tached and crushed and crashed down
into the lower levels. Intense excitement
prevailed through the town, as no one
could ascertain the extent of the fire or
the amount of the damage until late in
the afternoon, when some miners went
down through the Bodie Ind came
through the Standard at the 400 level.


They found that the fire had not gone
much below the 35O-foot level, and was
probably confined to the neighborhood
OF the Bulwer tunnel level. The new
electric hoist machinery is undoubtedly
destroyed.


The fire is still raging tonight, but under
control. The pumps are throwing good
stream down the shaft from the top of the
hill, and the Standard cyanide pump is
throwing water into the Bulwer tunnel.


This is the second loss by fire the Stand
ard Company has sustained within two
years, its large hosting works having
been DESTROYED in August. 1894.

The mail dock was busy again yester-
day. For a couple of days there have been
no steamers to work, and in consequence
the longshoremen have been disconsolate
The Gaelic, from Hongkong, via Yoko-
hama and Honolulu, was behind time, and
when shed get in last Sunday was placed
in quarantine. About noon yesterday she
was released, and had not yet left Angel
Island when the ,Zealandia came in from
Panama and way ports. Both steamers
got to the dock about the same time. but
the Zealandia was the only one TO put a
full force of men to work.


Although the Gaelic was released from
quarantine, her steerage passengers were
detained on the island and will not he
landed until this morning. The forward
and after matches were hermetcally sealed
after the fumigating apparatus had been
placed In them. The main hatch, in which
was rice and silks, was allowed to remain
open, and this was the only one from
which any discharging was done yester-
day. AT o'clock last night the matches
were removed and this morning q full
force OF men were at work.


The Zealandia will not make another
trip under the management of the Pacific
Mail and yesterday she was flying the
Oceanic Steamship Company's flag. After





go to Lombard-street wharf to make room
for the next Panama steamer. After dis
charging the remainder of her cargo she
will be turned over to the Spreckels Broth
ers Company and may be put in the sugar
trade, or she may be again laid up at
Martinez.


The Gaelic was caught in the same gale
that turned the Rio de Janeiro back. She
was three days late in reaching Yokohama,
but nevertheless there was plenty OF coal
III the bunkers to carry her to hongkong.
The story about the plague being aboard
her has been exaggerated and the officers
say that the man who died in Yokohama
may never have been passenger. Chinese
come and go in sampans at all hours while
the steamers are in port and any one OF
these may have been the victim. When
the Gaelic left Hong kong all the steeraee
passengers were examined, and before
Yokohama was reached they were exam
ined again. In these circumstances the
doctor does not think the plague could
have been aboard, more particularly as
there were nearly a thousand steerage
passengers and not another one showed
even the slightest symptoms. The disease
is very contagious.


The schooner Prosper returned to port
yesterday and went to Oakland Creek
direct. She left here on the 9th inst. and
two days ago in latitude 81 deg. SO min.
uOrtu, lOnSlIuue 10 ueS. ~ min. west,
sprang a leak and had to run back.
She was loaded with miners and mining
i'm plements for Cooks Inlet. After re.
pairing she will make another start, but
the chances are that many of her present
passengers will elect to remain at home.


The steam schooner Point Arena that
went on the rocks off the Mendocino coast
is slowly being towed to San Francisco by
the steam schooner South Coast. The un-
fortunate vessel has turned turtle and
when last seen off Stewarts Point she was
bottom up. The South Coast and her tow
may be expected this morning.


The news by the Gaelic goes to show
that Captain Philip Dryers slayer did not
live to be tried by legal court. After
shooting the skipper and wounding two OF
the Lyman D. Fosters crew, he set fire to
the vessel and jumped overheard. The

CLIFTON, KAN, April 27-Later details
from the scene of the cyclone Saturday
night do not change the figures in regard
to the loss of life. For distance of four
or five miles a space quarter of a mile
wide is covered with wreckage. In this
strip ten houses were demolished, six peo-
pie killed. two fatally injured and fifteen
hurt. Mrs. Bong, hearing the storm COM
ing, rushed into the pantry under the
stairway. She had barely got there when
the whole upper part of the house disap-
peared in the darkness. She remained In
the house all night and was found by the
neighbors in the morning calmly sittin G
amid the ruins.


Near this house in the track of the storm
stood the home of doctor called Indian
John. Two other men were in the house
at the time. Suddenly, without mo-
ment's warning, the house was crushed
like an eggsheil. but the men were un-
injured. In the home of Frank Peterson.
which was wrecked, were seven persons,
six of them members of the Peterson
family, and hired man. The house was
scattered over several acres, the barn
ruined and Peterson's wife and daughter
killed and all the others more or less in
iured. Just below Peterson's place lived
Ola Halverson. His home was taken to
the northeast. Not one stick upon an
other was left, and Halverson's wife was
killed and himself badly injured.


At the house of Charles Gardner the
family started for the cellar when the
roar of the storm was heard, but before
they got to the door the house was dashed
to pieces. Mr.. Gardner says:


II saw my wife pick up the baby and
then a crash came. remember nothing
more till I felt the rain falling on my
face. 1 arose and looked around. The
house had disappeared. 1 called to my
wife and she anowered, and going
toward her / found her with the
baby in her arms amid the frag-
ments of the house. She was uninjured,
and had the baby safe. One of my boys
was under part of the wall on one side
of the house. One of his legs was broken
below the knee. took stick and pried
him loose. My fve-year-old boy had dis
appeared, but after some search | found
him sixty rods from the house in the mud
not seriously injured


At Peter Anderson's, just across the val
ley from Gardeners, the wreck was even
worse, nothing being left but the cellar.
There were seven members in the family
The house was blown from over their
heads. Anderson soon found all the MEM
bers of his family except the child of his
daughter, five years old. The poor little
fellow was found in the morning dead.

SUMMIT, CAL, Sept. las freight
trsin No. 9 was approaching Summit last
evening, through the error of a brake
man, a life was sacrificed and two human
beings seriously injured. Train 9 had
orders to meet train at Summit. and No.
being eastbound and what is termed in
railroad parIance, an inferior train, had
to take siding. The switch was thrown
by brakeman, but the fatal error was
made by replacing the switch before all
the train had cleared the main line. Two
box cars and caboose still remained,
and both cars and caboose left the track,
the cars being thrown crosswise, blocking
the main line.


Wrecking crews were summoned from
Truckee, and the Summit section crew
was ushered into service. Train 4, car
rying European mail, would soon reach
Summit, and the brakemen iabored hero
ely to clear the wreck so as to cause her
little or no damage.


Thomas Casey, a laborer, was working
near one of the large posts which support
the snowsheds when, without moments
warning, the huge piece of timber,
loosened by the derailed cars, fell upon
his head, breaking his skull and laying
part of the brain bare. Another end of
the post struck two others, an Italian
named Pasquala and an American named
James Haggerty. Both are seriously in
iured, and even should they recover, they
will be disfgured for life. A special train
was dispatched with the unfortunate men
to the railroad hospital at Sacramento
A telegram received to-day says Casey
died without regaining consciousness.


Pasquala's wife reached Summit from
her home in Italy few hours alter the
accident occurred. She had not seen her
husband Tor nearly three years, and when
she was apprised of the accident and
realized that he was MANNED and Scared
for life she went into Mysteries. Attempts
to pacify her were of no avail, and she was
sent TO Sacramento on the next train.


The accident did not daunt the workers
who had escaped it. The track was rapidly
cleared and the European mail passed
through on schedule time.

They were provided with all the need

The land expedition was headed by
brave soldier, Gaspar de Portala, with
twenty-five soldiers, three muleteers and
many Indians. Father Juan Crespi and
Father Sierra were OF this party. To the
carefully kept diary of the former all our
California historians are greatly indebted,
while Father Serras name is indissolubly
linked with early California missions. He
was feeble in health and lame almost to
helplessness, but always cheerful, resolute
and heroic. Nearly forty days they
marched through desert and wilderness

the white sails of the San Car

them. Many of the Indians had de-

rescue. On Sunday they celebrated a
solemn festival, mass was said, cross set
up and formal possession taken of the land
for the church and for Spain.


So many of the men were sick that they
decided to send them back by the San An
tonic, while the rest divided into two par
ties, one staying at San Diego for mis-
sion work and one pushing north to Mon
terey.


Portala took command of the Monterey
expedition. After only five days of rest
he started north with Father Crespi and
siXty-four soldiers m uleteers and Indians.
They followed the coast line, Fastening on
through the pathless wilderness enduring
much hardship and keeping careful notes
of all they saw. They were charmed with
the climate and pleased with the poor ma
tives, who treated them with great friend
illness. Father Crespi baptized some of
the Indian children, giving them sweet
Christian names. at Los Angeles they
felt violent shocks of earthquake, but
they were not intimidated. The noun
tains seemed to rise interminably, but
they pushed on. They passed Monterey
Bay without recognizing it, and worn and
footsore reached San Francisco Bay, which
they named for their patron saint, name
never changed. Exhausted, sick, and
with scanty rations, they now decided to
turn back.


They reached Monterey the second time
November Is, 1869, and stopping at Carmel

abounded there. and the expected ships
from Mexico containing supplies had not

earnest prayer for succor, and loI the res

The Woodland Woolen-mills, owned by

immense structures cannot be saved. The

are valued at 900 and all will be lost.


At 2:30 O'Clock the work of destruction
was almost complete. The walls were fall
for miles around. Not thing has been
saved from the mills, the machinery and
stock on hand being destroyed.


The mill property was owned by Mrs.
Emma Laugenour, who holds an insur-
ance policy for $4,000 upon it. The
lessees, Shepherd & Collum, are insured
for $11, 900.


The wooden mills were Wood and's chief
industry, employing day and night
force of men, and being crowded TO their
full capacity. Their loss will be serious
blow to the town.


This was the second attempt to destroy
the mills made since yesterday morning,
and it has resulted successfully. The
first attempt was made just before
daylight yesterday. The torch was
applied, but the firebugs were frustrated

issuing from a sudden explosion.

coming through the floor. He broke two
hand-grenades, which had the effect OF
checking the flames, and the prolonged
screeching of the whistle brought assist
ance and the fire was effectually extin-

ROGERS. ARK, March 29.-One OF the
most horrible tragedies ever enacted IN
this part of the country occurred at the
home of Pulaski Duckworth, five miles
west of this place, about 10 O'Clock this
morning. Duckworth, who was an honor
able and respected citizen, and who had
always shown extreme love and care for
his family, while temporarily insane,
killed his wife, fatally wounded his i've
year-old daughter and then cut his throat,
dying instantly.


He struck his wife two blows with the
blade of an ak across the forehead, laying
her skull wide open. The woman see med
to have been struck first while standing.
The blow struck near the center of the
forehead and ranged downward.


The second blow took effect also in the
forehead and ranged diagonally across,
indicating that she was struck after falling
to the floor. The murderer then plunged
the bloody ak into the scalp of his five
year-old girl, laying her brain bare.


Leaving his victims writhing in their
blood, Duckworth went into another room.
and standing by the bed, cut his throat
with an ordinary pocketknife. the blade
being exceedingly dull. Both iugular veins
were severed and death resulted imme-
diately.


The little girl is yet alive, but her death
is expected at any hour.


The family consisted of Duckworth, his
wife, who was about 10 again become
mother, and two little girls, aged seven
and five years respectively.


The elder of the little girls, on her re-
turn from Sundayscbool, was borritied TO
find the bodies of her mother and sister
lying on the floor and writhing, and with
out looking for her father she ran to the
house of q neighbor about mile away for
assistance.


For some time Duckworth had been de-
spondent over his falling health. He had
just passed the meridian of life, his
strength had given way and he feared that
he would soon be unable to provide for his
family. He brooded over this until his
mind became un balanced, and rather than
see his loved ones suffer the pangs of hum
ger he com mitted the awful deed.

Judge Powell to-day issued restraining
order against Marie Wilson, Ruby Wilson

not to enter and to keep away from the
store of R. S. Raymond, where P. j.

persistently.

hindering, preventing and persuading
customers from purchasing goods.

from performing their duties. 1t is also
alleged that the women have frequently
come to the doors and windows of the
store and have Knocked, shouted at and
annoyed the plaintiff and his assistants,
and have made themselves offensive by
word and deed.


This suit grows out of the sensational

Harris, a stranger in this city, struck Miss

SALT LAKE, UTAH, Dec. 2l-The Su-
preme Court of this State tins afternoon
handed down unanimous opinion sus-
tanning the validity of the late election in
Utah. The election was contested princi-
pally on the grounds that the acts of the
Legislature regulating elections had not
been properly passed, for the reason that
the minutes of the legislative bodies did
not show that they had been passed by an
aye and no vote; also that the acts were
unconstitutional because they did not
fully conform to the State constitution in
regard 10 the form of the Australian secret
ballot system under which the election
was held. and that the use of party en-
blems on the ballots was illegal


The court held that the enrolled bills
signed by the presidents of both houses
and the Governor was the best evidence
that they had been properly enacted !;
that the ballot system was secret, the
method providing for tracing ballots be-
ing only applicable to fraudulent ballots,
and that party EN- blems on ballots were
proper. The decision is most important
one. If the court had held otherwise
Utah would have lost her Presidential
vote, had no Representative in Congress,
only ore United States Senator, no State
Legislature and the county officers elected
would have won futile victory.

role of his life this morning-that of ap.
pearing as witness against his bride OF
three days. The bride, too, filled not an
ordinary role-that of prisoner charged
with robbing the man who three days ago
made her his wife. Essie Winters was
the maiden name of Mrs. Stephen J..

THE CALL last Tuesday told the story of

The latter robbed Overton in the south

Under the law of this State husband

the Winters woman and Gould from the

This morning the case against Overton' s

| That little exception in the State law

untrue. She admitted that she was with

LEADvILLE, Col. Sept. 25.-The first
delegation of miners from Missouri ar
rived over the Denver and Rio Grande
at 1920 p. m. The train was q special and
was met at Malta, three miles out, by
the two new companies of militia organ
ICED this week and composed entirely of
business men and clerks They escorted
the train to the city, where it was met by
one-half of General Brooks command,
500 strong. with portion of the Chaffee
light artillery, two gatling guns and
cavalry troop. The seventy-five min
ers were surrounded by soldiers and the
cavalcade passed down Harrison avenue
to East Fifth street and thence out tow
ard the Emmett mine. Along the route
there were frequent yells of "scab" from
the strike sympathizers and the soldiers
were hooted at After leaving the ave-
nue. and getting into section where
many miners live the yells of "scab" and
jeering at the troops increased in vol
ume. At Orange street the cavalcade
halted for breathing spell and here the
enraged people grew more demonstra-
tive, crowding closely upon the troops
and showering abusive epithets alike
upon miners and militia. One of the
officers who was singled out by two men
for special abuse and crowding grew
angry and finally drew his sword, strik-
ing one Of his tormentors across the face
with the fat side ofthe sword and CIV
ing the other hard blow on the back as
he turned away. The command being
ready to move the order was given to
charge the crowd with gun butts and
push them back to give room for the
marching column. 1t was most well
come order and the celebrity with which
1t was obeyed sent panic through the
crowd who fed over fences and through
yards. Several windows of houses were
broken in by men blind with fear who
simply dashed away from the guns and
landed inside the windows with hands
and faces bleeding from the broken
glass. The march was then resumed
without further incident the miners
were soon safe inside the Emmett stock
ade and the escort Of militia returned to
camp. A cavalry patrol will be on guard
tonight which gives added confidence to
all.

SAN BERNARDINO, CAL, Aug. 49,
An unusual but not unprecedented atmos-
pneric condition obtained IN this region
to-day. The morning opened hot and
sultry, with light clouds hanging over the
mountain range. By noon the clouds
were of almost inky blackness and the
distant roar of thunder indicated that at
Squirrel Inn. the Little Bear Valley and
the Big Bear Valley the rain was falling
in torrents. An hour later the storm
clouds moved westward, and Mentone and
Redlands, at the head of the great valley,
were receiving a terrific downpour of
water.


The storm-ditches were overflowed, and
considerable damage was done to stores
and other pro perty in Redlands. 1t is re-
ported that many orchards were injured
by the rush of waters. In the highlands
trees were blown down and considerable
damage done to the growing orange crops.


In this city the rain fell for two hours
and wrought radical change in the tenn
perature. There was very little wind
here and no damage was done.


Not since August, 1891, has there been a
storm in midsummer that in extent and
severity approached to-day's visitation.
Undoubtedly the streams leading into the
Bear Valley reservoir, and all the streams
from which this valley draws water for
irrigation, have been vastly replenished.

A great many years ago there lived in
quaint old Monterey young Spanish
fisherman and his beautiful bride.


Every morning long ere the sun had
risen he and Juanita, his wife, went down
to the waters edge where the boats lay.
Now Juanita dreaded always to have him
leave her, even if only for day. for
she felt that the great blue sea might
carry him down, SO she was wont to
throw her arms around his neck
when the time for parting came
and beg him not to leave her; but Juan,
to quiet her fears, would jump gayly into
his boat and laughingly yet tenderly cry,
"Adios, my beautiful Juanita." Sitting
on the soft sand she watched. the tiny
boat until it was only speck. Then,
when the great sun climbed higher and
higher over the bay and the moon was
sinking out of sight, she sweetly sang:


Soft DER the fountain,


Lingering falls the southern moon;


Far oer the mountain
Breaks the day too soon.
Jumping mp she hastened to her little
adobe house, which stood on a hill over
looking the water, busying herself all day
with simple duties. Evening found her
again on the beach, waiting and watching
for her beloved Juan.


One happy morning lying beside them
was beautiful baby boy. AS they were
look ing with love upon him pure white
dove appeared and perched itself above
the boy.


Juan and Juanita were breathless and
soon all the town came to see the babe and
the white dove.


The parents were happier than ever
after their home had been SO blessed.


Their boy grew and was beautiful
child-so gentle and kind and loving that
the senores and senorltas called him "The
Angel Child"


No other name knew he, and the beauti-
full white dove was his constant compan-
ion, either perched on his shoulder or
hopping at his feet.


The angel child loved the calm blue
bay and was never SO happy as when the
great billows kissed his feet.


His soul was full of music and song and
almost every day he might be seen with
his mammals guitar, wandering through
the streets, over the hills and into the
woods, bringing forth sweet strains as he
went.


Years passed by-then a baby brother
came to the angel child. Happy he
was, indeed, and cried. "Oh, beautiful
mother, 1 shall show him my dearly
loved fairies of the woods. To the waters
edge I'll take him and summon forth the
water queen and her gay nymphs.
To his ear I'll hold my guitar and all
the music of the birds and the soft notes
of the trees and flowers and grasses he
will hear"


Juanita could say no word to her angel
child, for her heart filled with sadness,
while her eyes shone with love blinded by
her tears as she looked upon his sweet
face.


When another year had passed the baby
brother had gone; left the poor angel
child grieving. His guitar brought forth
no more notes OF joy and gladness.


1t was Christmas night. The rain fell in
torrents, while the great pillows from the
angry sea dashed against the rocks of the
shore.


Inside the tiny house "the angel child"
was going to God. In the next room, COO
ing and moaning, beating its wings against
the window-pane, was the dove, grieving
for its companion.
Ere the sun was in the east the sweet
spirit of the isherman's child had passed
away.


When Juanita left the bedside of her boy
she found the bird lying cold and stiff in
death.


The sorrowing ones placed the two side
by side, and over their grave hovers ever
snow-white dove. MAUDE WEsTPHAL.

Two Of Utica's young women cyclists, who
went to Clinton Saturday afternoon to sell
some tickets for the st. Agnes Church fair
and incidentally to witness the ball game
between Hamilton College and Syracuse
University teams on College Hill, had an ex-
perience which they will not soon forget.
At the conclusion of the game they thought
It would be great sport to coast down the
long and steep hill which leads from the
Oriskany valley to the college. Mounting
their wheels at the top OF the hill, they
placed their feet upon the rests, and set out
upon the descent, feat not INDUCED in by
even the best riders of the college or town.
1t was only a few seconds time before they
were moving down the hill at almost light.
ming rapidity, and those who witnessed their
descent and were aware Of their perilous po-
sition held their breath, expecting every
minute to see them dashed to pieces against
one of the many trees that line the sidewalk
from the top to the bottom Of the hill.


Entirely unconscious Of their danger, tho
young ladies sped on, their wheels assuming
greater velocity as they went. When in
front of President NJ. Woolsey Strikers resi-
dence the tire suddenly flew from the wheel
of one of the young ladies, and she was
hurled with great force on 10 the gravel
walk that leads to the presidents house.
Several who witnessed her accident hastened
TO reach her, expecting 10 ma net seriously
injured, and were much surprised 10 find
that, with the exception of few bruises on
her face, she was unhurt Her companion,
who was some distance ahead, needed the
advice of passing teams ter, and just before
the stone arbor was reached, turned her
wheel into the orchard that lies inst below
the residence of Prof. Edward North. She
proceeded until her wheel struck some OBJ
stacle, and then she was thrown several feet
further on down the side of the hill. Others
FASTENED to her rescue, and were not lit
tie surprised to find ner standing upon her
feet, apparently uninjured, beside her
wrecked wheel. Had she not steered her
wheel just she did, It is not improbable
that she would have collided with The stone
arbor and met an instant and frightful
death.


Persons who were driving down the hill at
the time and Witnessed the girls ana their
descent, say that they never expected to find
them alive. The sidewalk is only three or four
feet in width, and had they for a moment
realized their danger it is probable they
would have been seriously, II not fatally in
jured Their wheels were both badly broken,
and they took the evening train into the city.

on the Doorstep.


From the Philadelphia Press.


Commend me to the old lady in Roch-
ester who sought novel and successful
means of collecting. her house rent last
week. She vas an old lady of ideas and
a knowledge of human nature CLEANED from
a lifetime of experience with the world.
She owned a house and lot in Rochester
and the income from it was the substance
upon which she depended for hfe's necessi-
ties. 1t was rather an destinations house
and lot and the tenants were persons with
a reputation to sustain, although apparent
ly embarrassed for ready money Two
months rent was due, and the agent was
not able to collect.


She would collect it herself. Now, she
wasn't a stylish nor artistic old lady,
but she was sturdy and imperturbable, and
her proportions were ample and her spirit
unfaltering. She rang the door bell at an
early hour the other morning and inquired
for the head Of the family. The servant
glowered at her and said he was not to
be seen yet for two hours, because the fam
lily had not yet risen. The early caller was
cheerful. and said she'd sit on the door
steps and wait.


Finally she was granted an audience with
her tenant, who put her off with smooth
promises. I'll just sit here and wait till
you can pay it," replied the righteous col
lector, and she settled herself once more
on the door step, took some knitting from
her basket and prepared to spend the day
She made quain Unlocking picture, and
all the neighbors wondered. When any one
came within conversing distance and stared
rudely at her she explained in a friendly
way that she was waiting till the tenants
paid their rent. She looked truthful, and
no one doubted her, and her plan worked
like A charm. The rent was paid long be-
fore shutdown, and she ambled home more
than ever convinced that nothing is i'm
possible

at Del Monte, and the opening notes of

wooed the belated breakfasters from their

gent was busy arranging his wares in

amazed while the plaintiYe air they were

turned Immediately back into the office.

breath.


Finally, Frank Casserly, equipped with

PHOENIX, ARIz., Dec. 26.-The foot
ball eleven of the United States Indian
School near this city to-day won the
championship of the territory in game
with the Prescott eleven, which conquered
Phoenix yesterday. The game was hard
fought from beginning to end. Averaging
fifteen pounds less in weight than their
antagonists the copper-colored punters
put up dashing play and scored 20 to
Prescott's 6. They have lost but one game
out of four played this season.


The Indians averaged in weight 146
pounds; Prescott 161. The heaviest III
dian weighed 1863 pounds; the lightest 134.
The Indians did very little punting or
open playing, but relied on a revolving
wedge, which was something new 10 Pres
colt and could not be resisted. They were
also strong in interference and tackllng
and good runners. Their mass plays were
we'll executed and SO perfectly did they
play together that they had everything
their own way from the start. They
played fairly and came out without a
scratch.


The Prescott eleven did not fare so we'll.
B. f. Delanty, Campbell, Howard and
Coots were disabled in mass plays. The
Prescott men made game fight and ex-
ecuted some brilliant plays, but they could
not cope with the willy red men. Pritchett,
Trile and Marion were strong in tacklIng.
Captain Myers made a touchdown on a
beautiful halfback kick, which had never
been seen in Phoenix before. The Prescott
mass plays were principally OF the Penn
syivania tandem variety, and were gener-
ally successful. The team was weakened
by having four men disabled in the game
with Phoenix yesterday.


The Indian football team was organized
at the United States school by Superin-
tendent HARDWOOD Hall last year, and sew
eral matches were played with he Phoenix
eleven. The Pima boys seemed to possess
every qualification except confidence. The
games were all won by Phoenix. After
the Indians had a year of training under
Messrs. Cochran and Lesion, experienced
athletes, and conquered their timidity,
they became a formidable aggregation.
Four of the team that won to-day had
never played until this winter. The reds
had the advantage of the whites in giving
signals as they did not use cipher but
spoke in their native tongue.

WINSTON, N. c., Jan. 30.-Particulars
we're received here tonight of sensa-
tional fight between revenue officers and
moonshiners on Monday in Carroll
County, Va, near the North Carolina line
Deputy United States Marshal Worrel and
Deputy Collector William Thornton were
enticed by moonshiners TO go near the
Fancy Gap to cut up an illicit distillery.


When the officers arrived within about
100 yards of the still house they saw a num-
Der of men leaving there. The officers
called upon the supposed blocksders to
halt, whereupon the latter began firing
upon the officers, who returned the fire,
and fierce battle followed.


Marshal Worreu was shot down. His
deputy, Thornton, pleaded for some time
with the moonshiners before they would
allow him to care for Worrell.


One of the blockaders later assisted
Thornton in removing Worrell to an old
house. The deputy went after physi-
clan for his friend, but on his return the
moonshiners set upon him and beat him
numerically, if not fatally. Great indig-
nation exists over the affair.

NEW YORK, \. Y, Jan, 30.-George
Dixon, the famous feather-weight cham
pion, and "Peddler" Palmer. the no less
famous English bantam and conquerer of
Billy Plimmer, fought a six-round draw
at MadIson-square Garden in the presence
of about 6000 persons tonight. The con-
test was one Of the greatest exhibitions of
fast and scientific skill seen in many years.
Palmer scaled 1161& pounds. or a pound
lighter than his opponent, but to the eyes
of the onlookers Dixon looked much the
bigger man.


For the first two rounds the bantam out
pointed the feather-weight. Quicker than
fash be put in his left and ducked with
wonderful celebrity the fierce rushes and
heavy swings that have made Dixon ia
nous. Honors in the second and third
rounds were fairly even, but the last two
rounds were in the colored champions
favor. Palmer appeared to be firing and
the battering-ram attacks of Dixon scored.
The decision was enthusiastically received
and the sports cheered both the lads vo-
ciferously.


After few preliminary bouts had been
decided the stars of the evening appeared.
Dixon was first TO come into the ring.
Palmer followed shortly after and the
little Englishman was received with
storm of applause. The ''peddler'' looked
like mere child alongside his dusky OPP
poDent.


Palmer got to work quickly and sent the
left II on the jaw. He repeated on the
face a moment later and again on the
body. This neUtled Dixon and he made a
fierce swing which the EngIishman
avoided.


Dixon tried his famous rushing tactics
which brought the wonderful cIeEerness
of the ''peddler" out, and the colored cham
plon was iairly puzzled. Again and again
the colored lad tried to find an opening,
but Palmer eluded him easily. He ducked
TO either side with equal quickness and the
crowd rose en- masse and applauded his
clever work


Palmer sent a straight left on the jaw,
and IN rally fought George to the ropes
with both hands when the bell rang.


Both tried cautiously for an opening in
the second. Palmer got there first with a
left on the jaw. Dixon rushed, but failed
to score. The colored boy swung his left
Tor the jaw. but Palmer ducked and came
up smiling behind him. Dixon landed a
right on the jaw, and Palmer responded
with a left iab on the neck. They had a
hor rally in which Palmer had a bit the
better Oft, using both hands freely.


In the third round Palmer opened the
bail again, but Dixon swung the right
hand on the jaw. Palmer popped his left
on Georges chin and got away from hot
return. Tie 'peddler' forced the fight
ing with both hands ON the face and neck
but Dixon equalized with heavy body
blows, and honors were easy. Dixon was
the first to lead in the next, but fell short
and Palmer got in a straight left on the
neck. The cockney put light left-hander
in Dixon's face and got away cleverIy.
Dixon again played for the body, while
Palmer paid his attention to the feather
weights face. Just before the round
closed Dixon swung his right hard on the
'peddler's jaw and the blow told.


Palmer seemed to have lost some of his
wonderful quickness and Dixon's inning
commenced. Dixon swung his fight vi
ciously for the jaw and Palmer did not get
away quite fast enough, but did not get
the full swing Palmer jabbed aleft-hander
on Georges face, but did not phaze the
feather-weight any. Several hot exchanges
took place, and Dixon uppercut Palmer
with the left. Dixon landed the right on
the jaw with telling effect, and, though
Palmer tried his best, the round was
Dixon's.


Dixon opened the last with left swing
on the ear, followed up with right and
left on the face. Palmer clinched repeat
eddy and appeared tired. Once the Eng
ishman showed some of his form when
he sent his left into Dixon's face and got
away from the return. For the remainder
of the time Palmer was on the defensive.
Dixon crossed his right on the jaw, and
just before the bell rang the colored cham
pion swung a Highlander on Palmer's
jaw.


Referee Moore declared the bout a draw.

HAVANA, CUBA, March 18.-News has
been received here of an important battle
which was fought on Monday in the vicin-
lty OF Candelaria, in the Province of
Pinar del Rio. The Government troops
were unable to drive the insurgents back
and retired from their positions with con-
siderable loss.


The Spanish forces were commanded by
General Linares and Coionels Inclan and
Hernandez and the rebel forces by Maceo
and Bandera. The fight was begun on a
line parallel with the roadway. The Span
ish forces deployed the Tarifa Battalion, a
section of the Victoria Cavalry and de-
tachment of artillery forming the van
guard, and opened fire upon the enemy.
The rebels returned the fire, and at the
same time made an attack upon the rear
guard of the Spaniards, completely encir-
cling their column.


Having entirely surrounded the Govern
ment troops the insurgents advanced upon
the artillerymen with machetes. The
latter made vigorous resistance, using
muskets and grenades with such effect as
to check for time the enemy's advance;
but with re-enforcements second charge
was made by the insurgents and a hand
to-hand engagement ensued. The battle
terminated with bayonet charge. After
hot fight lasting two hours, the Span
iards were defeated, losing many killed
and wounded.


1t was the intention of the enemy to
prevent Colonel IncIan from proceeding
to Candelaria.


The official report of the fight says the
insurgents suffered tremendous loss. The
Spaniards lost two captains and FIVE pri-
Yates killed, and one lieutenant, four SER
geants and fifty-four soldiers wounded.
General Linares arrived at Caldelaria an
hour after the conclusion of the engage
ment, when he reported his share in the
battle.


Heliographic communication was inter-
rupted yesterday.

houses in San Antonio de las Vegas, in the

Seven gig crews from the British ships

worried over the vexed problem as to
which crew was the better oarsmen.


The race was held under the auspices of
the British Sailors Institute and the Rev.
Mr.. Fell acted as referee and starter.


The course over which the race was rowed

the bark Alexander, anchored off the sugar
refinery, and back to stakeboat abreast
of the Union Iron Works. All in all, the
course was about a mile and half in
length.


Boats from the following ships took part
in the regatta: Arctic Circle, British Yoe-
man, Cromdale, Ellesmere, Varajein,
Incheape Rock and Balamere.


AT the word "go" the gig crew from the
lnchcape Rock caught the water first and
got slight start. The other boats started
of simultaneously, and hot race ensued
to the turning boat, with the Inchcape
Rock crew boat length in the lead. and
the others so well punched that daylight
was invisible between.


A foul occurred in the race to the turn
ing point between the crews of the Vara-
jein and Celtic Race, but little ground was
lost through it, and nearly all the boats
rounded the bark Alexander together with
the Inchcape Rock crew still in the lead.


Coming home with the tide all the
crews redoubled their efforts, and a most
exciting finish was the result. But the
Inchcape Rocks gig proved the winner by
fifteen seconds, with the British Ieoman
second and the Cromdale third.


TIE other boats finished within half a
boats length of each other.


A large crowd witnessed the race, prin-
cipally friends OF the apprentice boys and
of the institute.


On the bark Alexander, at the turning
point was crowd of the fair sex, who be-
came very enthusiastic when the boats
started to turn and urged their favorites to
do their utmost to win.


After the race was over the crew of the
Inchcaps Rock boat was presented with
$40, and somptuous repast was spread
for them when they went aboard their
ship.


The coxswains of the boats in the race

amount of interest was manifested in the
contest. 1t has been one of the topics Of
conversation around cline juice" corner,
Battery and Washington, for the past
week.

nightly for the event, and quite sum OF
money chan ed hands on the result.


The outcome of this race will be another
regatta, to be held at Sausalito in two
weeks in which it is expected that the
crews from nearly all the British ships in

CHICAGO, ILL, Dec. 12.-Every open
poolroom in this city was raided by the
police this afternoon and the number OF
prisoners taken is larger than in any rad
made here in months. Warrants were
taken out for the thirteen poolrooms
which were recently opened here, but
only five were found open when the police
arrived. These were filed with patrons
and more than three hundred prisoners
were taken to the station: The keepers
were arrested under State warrants, while
the patrons will be arraigned as inmates.
Bail was quickly obtained, and within
three hours from the time the raid was
begun all of the prisoners had been re-
leased. 1t is said that the managers will
refuse to close their doors in order that a
test case may be made.


They claim that they are not operating
in violation. although Chief Badenoch is
acting with the advice of the law depart
ment and says that he will raid the places
as fast as they are opened. Notification

five ignored it.

the usual incidents. Ten patrol wagons
were brought into service and nearly
twenty loads of prisoners were taken to
the station. At Powers & O'Brien's
place on Madison street the appearance
of the police caused intense excitement
and about thirty of the inmates escaped
while the officers were guarding the doors.
The poolreom is on the second floor and
many escaped by means of the dummy
elevator through which drinks are sent
up from the saloon before the police dis
covered it. Many others escaped down
fire escapes and several ran past the po-
| lice in the doorways.

| however, are investigating and believe

this city. They expect to find an instru-
ment somewhere in Chicago which was


used to induce the people to believe that


the kilograms were sent abroad and the


place of agreement therefore was not

BOSTON, MASS, Dec. 25.-The overdue
Allen line steamer Scandinavian from
Glasgow arrived to-day, six days late,
owing to bad weather, poor coal and green
firemen.


On Christmas eve she collided off Cape
Cod with the undertaken schooner Carrie
Walker, which vessel became a total
wreck, as the result of the collision, her
crew of six men being brought here on
the steamer. The accident was due to the
steam ship captain mistaking the
schooner for the pilot-boat on the Cape
Cod station as she burned fare-up lights
used aboard the pilot feet as signal
Chief Mate Aitken answered what he
thought TO be pilot-boat's signal. The
wind was blowing from the north north
aest, which being fair wind for the sail
ing craft, the latter commenced to draw
nearer the steamer, and the steamer kept
her course at moderate rate of speed,
naturally thinking that the supposed pilot
boat. would come about and launch a boat,
instead of which the schooner crashed
into the steamer with terrific force, strik-
ing her on the starboard bow and doing
considerable damage. The schooner's
yawlboat brought the crew to the steamer.
The Scandinavian has two holes in her
starboard bow, one about two feet square
just above the load-line, while the other is
on the bluff of the bow. where a large
piece of the schooner's iibboom and por-
tion of her jib had lodged.


The schooner Carrie Walker was COM
manded by Captain Starkey, owned by
Charles w. King of Eastport, Maine, and
left st. Johns, N. B., December Is, with
laths and shingles for New London, Conn.
Captain Starkey says: when the col
lision occurred the vessels bows opened
and filled rapidly with water and she
must have capsized, az she was nowhere
to be seen shortly afterward. Flare-up
light was used simply to warn the APP
preaching steamer, which should have
given US the right of way, according to
the rules Of the road at sea. The crew
had barely time to gather their trunks
and personal effects and stow them aboard
the yawl before leaving the wreck"

II shall never forget sitting up all night

hours he told of his adventures.


"One story of London landlady

las demanded the best she had. and the

sat down to write and smoke.


"Soon lackey observing him from the

Senator, detecting impertinence in the
mans manner. smoked on. Another
came, and still he smoked. Then a man
in tall coat and white gloves entered
and was very peremptory. Douglass
looked at him and pulled away Then
the stout little landlady appeared with all
her feathers flying and began to lay down
the law.


This time Douglas rose and faced the
intruder Summoning all the grandeur of
manner which had captured audiences and
quelled conventions, he bowed pro oundly
and said, with resonant voice and solemn
pause, Madame, perhaps you do not know
who l amp


1.-The lady confessed her ignorance.


...Madame, said Douglas-and no one
could do it better-'I am an American
sovereign


1.-The round little lady courtesied and
backed ont of the room. And when Sir
Robert Peel called the next day. and car
riages of lords and notables blocked the
way, she decided that she was harborin g
sovereign, indeed, and that there were
not lackeys enough under her roof to do
him honor" Times-Herald.

OMAHA, NEBR., Dec. 2.-Burglsrs broke
into the safe of the Nebraska Loan Office
last night and looted its safe of $4,000
worth Of watches. diamonds and jeweIry.


Precautions taken by the burglars to
avoid detection were as novel as ingenius.
Adjoining the pawnshop on the east IS a
vacant store building. The front door was
opened with skeleton key, although
there are indications that chisel may
have been used. From the store the
bur glars worked their way into the pawn
shop by tearing off the plaster between
the studcings aud making hole large
enough to crawl through. A small hole
was bored through the wall between the
vacant store and the pawnshop, IN the
vicinity of the safe. a string about fifty
feet long was passed through the hole,
one end of which was held by guard at
the front. while the other was so arranged
as to communicate with the burglars at
work upon the safe.


The guard could peer through the
frozen plate-glass windows upon Douglass
street, watch the movements of the police
and passing pedestrians who might inter-
fere with the robbery, and warn his pals
in time TO escape through the rear door.


The safe-door knob was knocked of, and
hole drilled through the lock controlling
the big bolt which manipulated the
tumblers. A punch displaced the lock,
and the big safe doors opened without the
use of explosives or creating any noise.
The inside doors were operated similarly,
with the result that the contents OF the
safe, representing about $4,000, were at the
disposal of the robbers.


Eleven trays of watches, diamonds and
jewelry were emptied, and the robbers
disappeared without leaving any clew.

HIGHLAND LIGHT, NJ ASS, Sept. IA
The Italian bark Monte Tabor, loaded with
salt, went on Peaked Hill bar at mid
night and shortly after began TO break up.
The crew became panic-stricken. Even
the officers lost their wits.


The captain, F. Dellacassa, evidently
considering himself responsible for the
loss of the vessel, shot himself in the head
with a revolver and fell dead to the deck,
whence his body was soon afterward
washed into the sea.


The mate, believing death to be newt
able and afraid of drowning, drew his
razor across his throat, producing
CHASTITY wound and falling dead into the
water beside the doomed bark.


The crew, twelve in number, chung to
the deckhouse. expecting every minute to
be the last. The vessel held together for
about an hour and then went to pieces.
The twelve men went over the side still
clinging to the deckhouse. Five of them.
however, were unable to maintain their
hold and were soon drowned. The sur
vivors reached the shore in an exhausted
condition and were taken TO the Peaked
Hill life-saving station, where they were
cared for.


The body of the mate was washed
ashore at Race Point at o'clock. An
hour and a half later two other bodies
were found on the shore One of these
men had followed the example of the mate
and had cut his throat before being swept
into the sea.


The Monte Tabor sailed from Trapani
July 81 for Boston.

WICHITA, KANs., Jan. 7.-Portions of
Kiowa, Stafford, Edward and Pratt coun-
ties are being swept by prairie fires which
light up the sky until from the distance
its appearance is that of red sunset.
The extent of the destruction has not been
definitely learned, for the reason that the
desolated country is entirely cut off from
telegraphic communication.


The branch of the Missouri Pacific Rail-
road from Alcott west, which runs through
the fre-swept district, has been abandoned
for several months and all telegraph offices
along the line discontinued, hence the de-
tails obIainable are very meager.


There is no telegraphic communication
with Iuka, in Pratt County, on the aban-
doned branch, but reports from Dodge
City, Kinsley, Stafford, st. John, Larned
and other surrounding towns lead to the
apprehension that the town has been
swept away.


Thousands of acres have been burned
over, and the loss of property will be con-
siderable. Ten years ago, while Kansas
was having its wonderful boom, the

across. At great risk of life and with al

Two Methodist bishops were deposed

stress Of long debate, Bishops Bowman

10 the history Of the church. For twenty.
four years the two bishops held autocratic
power and shaped the destinies Of thou.
sands Of ministers. They said &C.," and
the travelling preacher went. They said
Remain" and he moved not. From the
pedestal Of supreme authority the general
conference, which gave them their power,
took 1t away because years had sapped
their vital forces and impaired their use.
fitness. When the committee on episco.
pacy announced the warrant for their
official death the white.haired bishops,
who had striven 80 long for the glory OF
their God and their church, In voices
choked with emotion pleaded the privilege

the warrant was being put into execution.

to save them their honors and emoluments
and relieve them Of excessive duties, but
the general conference voted to choose

SEATTLE, WASH, May 1.-The schoon-
ers Lakme and Utopia, about which so
much anxiety has been felt for fortnight
past, reached Sitka safely, and if disaster
has overtaken either or both it was after
the vessels had sailed from that far
northern town for Cooks Inlet.


The steamer Mexico brought the good
news. When the vessel arrived in port
this morning at $50 o'clock there were
many anxious mothers, wives and sweet
hearts on the dock eagerly waiting for
authentic information. good or bad.
When at last the spell was broken many
wept for Joy and some Trailer ones suffered
physical collapse.


The Lakme reached Sitka without
serious mishap April and proceeded the
same day toward Cooks Inlet. The
Utopia got in on the 10th and sailed the
following day. Since then nothing has
been heard from either vessel and while
both are now overdue at this port it is not
felt that there is occasion for alarm at the
delay. They may be detained even two
weeks longer on account of the ice in the
inlet, which Captain Wallace of the
Mexico says prevails to far greater
extent this year than he has ever known
before.

students and the 135 students now receiv-
ing daily instructions. Mr.. Mcclure then
read the names Of the successful ones, and
gave them the prizes, after which they re-
ceived the warm congratulations of their
friends assembled to hear the verdict. The
exhibition at the school opened today, and
will be open until Saturday noon.

SAN DIEGO, CAL, March 6.-Four lit
tie children, the oldest under ten years,
started alone to-day for Charleston. H.,
with the corpse of their mother. They
boarded the Chicago Limited and took
seats among number of strangers, who
were laughing and chatting. There was
no indication in the faces of the men and
women that death was near. Outside on
the platform there was rafting and
banging of trunks and the usual noise of
railway station. Baggagemen tenderIy
picked UP a long box and placed it among
the trunks in the forward car, the remainder
of the trunks and valises were piled in,
and the conductor looked again at his
watch as the time for departure neared.


Everybody seemed to be lighthearted,
but the children were sad-faced, and
the youngest. a 3-year-old tot, began to
cry for its mother. The eldest girl wiped
away the little ones tears and spoke COM
forting words, although the spring of her
own sorrows was full TO overfiowing.


A man and woman entered the car with
the little ones and endeavored to make
them cheerful, but they could not bring
smiles to the sad faces, though the
tears were dried. When the conductor
shouted" All aboard !''the man and woman,
their own eyes filled with tears, hurried
out to the platform, after giving the little
ones farewell kiss. The engine started and
soon the last coach was out of sight around
the bend at Cedar street. The man and
woman watched it as far as they could see
any part of the train and then turned
away. Poor little things" they said.


The four little children were those of
Mrs. Ada Mathes, who died at 234 Grand
avenue on Wednesday from consumption.
She had come here five weeks ago from
Charleston, ILL.,, with her children, and
when she died the little ones were left
alone, and alone they are going with her
remains to Charleston.


The father of the little children had be-
longed to fraternal organization, and
the members of the organization did
everything they could to make the or
phans comfortable. kilograms were sent
ahead to-day to lodges along the road re-
questing that the travellers be looked after,
and it is probable that they will be well
cared for along their homeward way.

MADRID, SPAIN, Feb. 10.-An aerolite
burst over the city of Madrid this morn
ing, causing great CONSERVATION among
the inhabitants. The first warning of the
explosion was a fash which illuminated
the sky, which was almost Immediately
followed by a tremendous report, the vi
brations from which shattered hundreds of
windows. The aerolite was accompanied
by great white cloud and simultaneous
with the explosion there was trembling
of the earth resembling the sensation pro-
duced by an earthquake.


When the flash and ensuing report took
place the people rushed panic-stricken
into the streets and some minutes elapsed
before the excitement was allayed. It is
estimated that the meteoric body was
twenty miles above the earth when it
burst.

SAN BERNARDINO, CAL, July 25.-
About eighty miles north of Mojave is an
institution known as the San Bernardino
Borax Works. In the years before the
enactment of the Wilson-G German tariff
law, about 100 men were employed at
the works. each receiving not less than
$50 month and board. There were six
drivers of mule teams, which freighted
the borax to Mojave. These received SIPS
per month for their services and the
swampers about the marsh received $85.
Five stations were established between the
works and Mojave, with large farms and
houses where number of people were
employed at good salaries. A trip from
the borax WORKS to Mojave was made
every eight days with three twenty-five
mule teams, hauling sixty tons, from
which was realized, under the Mckinley
law, $400 per ton.


To-day borsx would bring but $50 per
ton, because of the withdrawal of the pr O.
lection afforded by the Mckinley tariff.
Under present conditions, of course, the
works have closed and hundreds of men
are. thrown out of employment. The
busy whirl of machinery has ceased.


The big wagons are no longer used, and
the mules have been sold, given away OF
are idly "eating their heads off," The
shouts Of men have died away. A keeper
takes care of the company's property, and
the owners are awaiting the return of pro-
lection and the prosperity sure to follow
the election of William Mckinley and g
Republican Congress. Then the works
will be reopened.

GRANTS PASS, Or, Oct. 6.-Two wild
engines running without orders on the
Southern Pacific between Roseburg and
billiards coilided in a dense fog on curve
half mile from Greens station at $50
o'clock this morning. John McGonigle of
Portland, freuan of the southbound
engine, and Albert N. Toish of Salem,
brakeman who was on the engine, were
instantly killed. Five trainmen were
badly injured. They are: James Porter,
engineer on the northbound engine,
severely bruised and one ankle broken;
George Happersette, fireman on the north
bound engine, both legs broken and feet
crushed, rendering amputation of one leg
below the knee and the other foot neces-
sary; Benjamin Lohr, head and face cut;
Fred Wall, conductor, on Porter's engine,
bruised and cut about face and head;
Engineer McCalley, badly bruised.


Conductor Wall of the overland bound
for San Francisco accidentally left his
tickets and papers at Roseburg this morn
ing. He could not well proceed without
them, so he sidetracked at Billiards and
taking his engine started back to that city.
In the meantime Conductor Wallis papers
were discovered by the station agent at
Roseburg and the train-dispatcher ordered
out light engine to overtake the overland
about Myrtle Creek keeping a lookout for
No. 10 and section men.


The morning was densely foggy and
while rounding a curve the engines
crashed into each other. Both were going
at full speed and travelling backward. So
great was the force of the impact that all
the occupants were thrown into the air
and the two tenders wrecked. Tigh and
McGonigle were instantly killed.


Engineer Porter had reversed his engine
before being thrown from the cab. The
locomotive broke from the tank and ran
southwsrd couple of miles. where it was
found exhausted. The tanks of both en-
gines were badly demolished.


The first news of the accident was
brought to town by farmer on horseback.
Division Superintendent Fields, who ar
rived this morning from Portland, went
Immediately to the scene of the wreck
with physicians and brought back the in
lured men, returning with 8 Coroner. The
Coroner's jury heard some evidence this
afternoon, and, owing TO the condition OF
the injured men, adjourned the hearing
until tomorrow morning.

TACOMA, VASE, July 1s.-Jennie
Flanagan, 17-year-old girl who lives on
farm near Ethel, Lewis County, claims
she has been twice attacked by strange
man in the past two months. The stranger
visited the house month ago in the
absence of her father. His appearance
frightened the girl and she attempted to
escape. but he seized fatiron and told
her that if she made an outcry he would
kill her. She reached for q hunting
knife, but the man was too quick and
secured the knife himself. Just then the
family watchdog entered the house and
the stranger beat hasty retreat, shouting
as he ran that she had not seen the last of
him.


Miss Flanagan saw nothing more of the
man until Wednesday. Then, while she
was walking twenty rods from the house,
he suddenly stepped from the brush and
caught her by the hair. A hard struggle
followed, and he dragged her by the hair
for several rods. He was again scared
away by the dog, but in the struggle he
tore the girls dress oil.


Sheriff Carpenter and Deputy Black
we'll, when notified of this second attack,
made thorough search in the surround
ing woods, but could find no trace of the
girls assailant. According to Miss
Flanagan, the stranger has red hair that
reaches to his shoulders. The neighbour
hood has been greatly aroused by the
girls story.

bidders were the Sun, the Times Index,

act.

Injunction proper was served too late,

size, depth and color, are lovely stones.

brought into the market, and those SOLD

modern fashion.

space. The chrysoprase is pretty, but
